Do squatters have rights to a house in Missouri?

A person living in a house they do not own can eventually claim title in Missouri, but only by holding it for the full statutory period. Since August 2024 the owner also has a fast court route to remove someone who entered without permission. Both pieces of law matter if you own a vacant or inherited house.

The long route is adverse possession. It rests on section 516.010, which bars anyone from suing to recover land or its possession unless they, or the people they claim through, held or possessed the premises within ten years before the suit. A court decides whether an occupant's use measured up.

The short route is a removal petition under section 534.602, enacted through H.B. 2062 in 2024. It targets people who occupy a residential dwelling with no permission and no legal right to be there.

How long someone must occupy land to claim it

The base period is ten years under section 516.010. The statute is written as a limit on the owner's right to sue, not as a recipe for the squatter, so court decisions fill in what an occupant must show:

  • The occupant must hold with the intent to possess the land as their own. A 1958 decision treats intent to possess, not intent to take from the true owner, as what makes the holding adverse.
  • Open, continuous and uninterrupted use for the full period creates a presumption that the use was adverse, but a 1956 decision holds that the presumption disappears once there is some substantial evidence that the use was permitted.
  • Possession that began with the owner's gift can be adverse from the start, as a 1958 decision found.
  • Surface possession alone cannot carry title to a mineral estate that was already severed (1984).

A second rule, section 516.070, covers land whose equitable title came from the government more than ten years earlier. If the possessor is in lawful possession, the other claimant has not been in possession for thirty consecutive years and neither has paid any taxes in that time, the claimant gets one year to sue before being barred, and title vests in the possessor.

What an owner can do right away about unauthorized occupants

File a verified petition in the county where the house stands. Under section 534.602, the court must immediately issue an ex parte order to remove the occupant if the petition shows good cause, and a hearing follows within forty-eight hours of filing unless good cause justifies a delay. The sheriff then enforces the order by removing the occupant from the property.

The petition has to state a set of facts, and an owner who cannot truthfully state them should use another route:

  • The petitioner is the owner or the owner's authorized agent, and the property includes a residential dwelling.
  • The occupants entered and remain without permission, and the property was not open to the public when they entered.
  • They are not guests, and the owner told them to leave and they refused.
  • The property has not been leased to anyone for three consecutive months, and the occupants are not current or former tenants.
  • The occupants are not the owner's immediate family, and no litigation about the property is pending between the owner and any of them.

Filing fees and court costs match those for a claim in associate circuit court, and the circuit clerk must explain the filing procedure to an owner without a lawyer, free of charge.

Sheriff removal and the risks of getting it wrong

After the sheriff serves the order, the owner may ask the sheriff to stand by while the locks are changed and the occupants' belongings are moved to or near the property line. Subsection 11 of section 534.602 lets the sheriff charge a reasonable hourly rate for that standby, and the person asking pays it. The sheriff is entitled to the same fee as for serving a writ of possession under section 57.280.

The statute also protects occupants against abuse. Someone removed without just cause may sue for restored possession, actual damages to personal property, statutory damages of $1,000 and court costs. Those damages are reduced by any damage the removed person did to the real property, which the owner must prove. The petition turns on facts about permission and leasing, so gather dates and any messages before you file.

Separately, section 569.200 makes it the crime of criminal mischief, a class A misdemeanor, to unlawfully detain, occupy or trespass upon a residential dwelling, and section 534.602 lets the sheriff arrest anyone found in the dwelling for trespass, warrants or other legal cause.

Squatter or holdover tenant?

A tenant who once had permission is handled under the unlawful detainer statute, not the new removal petition, which requires that the occupants are not current or former tenants. Section 534.030 defines unlawful detainer to include willfully holding over, without force, after a lease ends, and wrongfully taking and keeping possession without force, then refusing to leave after a written demand from the person entitled to possession.

Missouri routes for removing an occupant, by who the occupant is
OccupantRoute
No permission, no lease, dwelling not rented in 3 monthsVerified petition and ex parte removal order
Tenant holding over after lease endsUnlawful detainer action
Possessor refusing a written demand to leaveUnlawful detainer action
Former tenant after a foreclosure saleNotice with at least ten business days to leave, then court action
Anyone unlawfully occupying a dwellingCriminal mischief, class A misdemeanor

If you are unsure which category applies, ask the clerk at the circuit court in your county. Clerks must explain filing procedures, and the Supreme Court supplies the forms.

Protecting a vacant house and selling it cleanly

Visit it, keep records, and deal with any occupant early. The ten year clock in section 516.010 only helps someone whose use was open, continuous and hostile for the whole period, so regular inspections and a dated written demand to leave give you a paper trail. Section 534.030 itself relies on a written demand.

An occupant who stays and later claims title can start a suit under section 527.180, which lets the holder of title by limitation ask the circuit court of the county to perfect the record title. The decree can be recorded with the recorder of deeds. Only people with an adverse record claim need to be named as defendants.

Owners who want out of a house with occupants, back taxes or repair problems can sell as is, but a buyer's title company will ask who lives there. Settle that first, using a petition or a notice as your facts require, and read our Missouri eviction notice guide if a tenant is involved. Photos with dates, utility records and a log of your visits all help show that the house was never abandoned to anyone.

Frequently asked questions

How many years of adverse possession does Missouri require?

Ten years is the base period under section 516.010, which bars a suit to recover land unless the plaintiff or those they claim through held it within ten years. A longer thirty year rule in section 516.070 applies to certain land.

Can I remove a squatter from my Missouri house without a tenant eviction?

Yes, on the right facts. Section 534.602 lets an owner file a verified petition for an ex parte removal order if the occupant has no permission, was never a tenant and the home has not been leased for three months.

Is squatting a crime in Missouri?

Unlawfully detaining, occupying or trespassing on a residential dwelling is criminal mischief, a class A misdemeanor, under section 569.200. The sheriff may also arrest an occupant for trespass or outstanding warrants.

What if I remove someone and a court says I was wrong?

The person removed without just cause can sue for restored possession, actual damages to personal property, $1,000 in statutory damages and court costs. Damage they did to the house is offset.

Does paying property tax matter to a squatter's claim in Missouri?

Section 516.070 turns partly on whether either side paid taxes for thirty years. For the ten year rule in section 516.010, courts look at the nature of the possession, and tax payment is one fact among others.

What landlord tenant law means when you sell a rental

The lease, the deposit and the way a tenancy ends all travel with the house, so know where each stands before a buyer gets involved. Missouri has no single landlord-tenant code. The rules sit in Chapters 441, 534 and 535 of the Revised Statutes.

A rental that is sold keeps its tenant. The buyer steps into a house with a lease already running, a deposit already held and perhaps a month-to-month renter who can be given notice only in writing. The first piece of paperwork to plan for on a Missouri sale is a written notice to the tenants of the change to a new landlord.

An owner selling to a buyer who wants the property vacant has a different job. You cannot simply ask a tenant to leave on the closing date. The notice period, the type of tenancy and the court process all have to be respected, and the sections below walk through each.

Security deposit limits

A landlord may not demand or receive more than two months of rent as a security deposit. Under RSMo 535.300, the money must sit in an insured bank, credit union or similar depository, and any interest it earns belongs to the landlord. A deposit labeled as a pet deposit falls outside the statutory definition.

When the tenancy ends, the landlord has thirty days to do one of two things: return the full deposit, or mail the tenant an itemized written list of the damages withheld together with whatever balance remains. Mailing to the tenant's last known address counts as compliance. Before deducting anything, the landlord must give the tenant reasonable written notice of a move-out inspection time, and the tenant may attend.

The allowed deductions are narrow:

  • unpaid rent owed under the rental agreement;
  • restoring the unit to its starting condition, with ordinary wear and tear excluded;
  • carpet cleaning, only if the lease set that charge in advance and warned the tenant, with a receipt for the actual cost due within thirty days;
  • actual losses from a tenant who left without giving adequate notice, provided the landlord tried to limit those losses.

A landlord who wrongfully keeps any part of the deposit owes the tenant twice the amount withheld. Before you sell, settle the deposit ledger cleanly, ask your closing agent how the deposit will pass between you and the buyer, and put the answer in writing.

How a tenancy ends and how much notice is required

A tenancy with no written, signed lease is treated as month to month, and either side can end it with one month of written notice. RSMo 441.060 says the termination date must fall on a periodic rent-paying date at least one month after the notice is received. Oral notice from either party is not valid, and a lease running a year or longer must be written and signed.

A written lease ends on the date it names, and neither side owes the other notice unless the lease has an automatic renewal clause. A tenant who stays past the end date without a written agreement can be charged double rent. A tenant who sublets without the landlord's approval can also face double rent.

Three other rules can matter on a sale:

  • Mobile home lot tenancies shorter than a year need sixty days of landlord notice, counted from the date the next rent payment comes due.
  • An occupancy limit of two people per bedroom is presumed reasonable, though it does not apply to a child born to the tenants during the lease.
  • An active-duty service member may end a lease on 15 days' notice after a permanent change of station, certain long orders, discharge, or an order to government quarters, and is entitled to a full deposit refund if the other lease terms were met.

Removing a tenant takes a court order

A landlord may not evict a tenant without a court order. Grounds for starting a case include unpaid rent, property damage, a lease violation, staying past the end of the term, drug-related activity, illegal gambling and allowing a person the landlord previously excluded to live there. The tenant receives notice of the lawsuit and a chance to be heard before any removal.

After a judgment, RSMo 441.060 sets a self-help path with strict conditions. If the officer holding the writ has not delivered possession within seven days, the landlord has sixty days from the judgment to enter without breaching the peace, in the presence of a local law enforcement officer who has been shown the judgment and execution order and acknowledges that in writing. That acknowledgment must be filed with the court within five days after possession is taken.

Shutting off water, power or gas to push a tenant out is a different matter. A landlord who willfully interrupts utility service commits forcible entry unless the interruption is for health and safety reasons. If a rental is lost to foreclosure, RSMo 534.030 gives a residential occupant a notice from the new owner and at least ten business days before any possession suit can start.

Tenant repair rights

Missouri tenants have very little room to withhold rent. In most circumstances a tenant has no right to hold back payment, and doing so can lead to eviction. The one narrow exception is repair and deduct under RSMo 441.234.

That section applies only to a tenant who has lived in the unit six consecutive months, has paid all rent and charges, and has not received an uncured written lease or house rule violation notice. The condition must hurt habitability, sanitation or security and violate a local housing or building code. The repair cost must be under $300 or half of the periodic rent, whichever is greater, and never more than one month's rent.

The tenant notifies the landlord, waits fourteen days, and then may have the work done and deduct the documented cost. If the landlord disputes the need in writing, the tenant needs a written certification from the local government that the code is violated before doing the work. Total deductions cannot exceed one month's rent in any twelve months, and a lease cannot waive these rights. If you plan to sell, clear any open repair request first, because a pending code issue gives a buyer's inspector something to cite.

Missouri rental rules at a glance

Missouri rental rules for a seller to check
TopicRule
Security deposit capTwo months of rent
Deposit return30 days after the tenancy ends, with an itemized list if any is kept
Penalty for wrongful withholdingTwice the amount withheld
Month-to-month noticeOne month, in writing
Mobile home lot, lease under one year60 days from the next rent due date
Repair and deductUnder $300 or half of one month, whichever is greater; 14 days after written notice
Foreclosed rental occupantAt least 10 business days after the new owner's notice
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Missouri houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Before you sell a Missouri rental

Start by pulling the signed lease, the deposit record and any written notices already sent to the tenant. Then match the end date of the tenancy against your target closing date. A month-to-month tenant who has not been given a proper written notice can stay, so a buyer who wants an empty house needs the notice served early enough to land on a rent-paying date.

  • Confirm whether the deposit sits in an insured account and what it totals.
  • Send the tenant written notice of the ownership change.
  • Close out any open repair request and keep the receipts.
  • Hold a move-out inspection only after giving the tenant reasonable written notice of the time.
  • Follow fair housing rules when talking with prospective buyers or tenants. Race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status and national origin are protected, and the Missouri Human Rights Commission at 877-781-4236 takes complaints.

If the tenant will stay, a buyer who wants an investment rental may take the house with the lease in place. If the buyer wants it empty, the notice dates above set the pace, and a cash buyer who accepts the house as it stands can sometimes close without waiting for the tenant to leave.

Frequently asked questions

Does a tenant's lease survive the sale of a Missouri rental house?

The lease stays in place unless it ends by its own terms or by proper notice. Missouri gives a seller no way to cancel a lease because a sale is coming. Plan on sending the tenants a written notice of the ownership change at or before closing.

What is the most a Missouri landlord can charge as a deposit?

Two months of rent is the ceiling under RSMo 535.300. Money a tenant pays specifically as a pet deposit is outside the statutory definition of a security deposit, so the cap and the thirty-day return clock apply to the general deposit.

Can I give a month-to-month tenant a verbal notice to move?

No. Oral notice from either party is not valid. A month-to-month tenancy ends only through a written notice that names a rent-paying date at least one month after the other side receives it.

Can I change the locks or cut the utilities to speed up a sale?

No. A landlord needs a court order to evict, and willfully interrupting water, electricity or gas is forcible entry unless done for health and safety. After a judgment, entry is allowed only under the conditions in RSMo 441.060, including a law enforcement officer's written acknowledgment.

Can a tenant deduct repair costs from rent?

Only in a narrow case. The tenant must have lived there six months, be current on rent, face a code-violating condition that affects habitability, sanitation or security, and give the landlord fourteen days after written notice. The deduction is capped by RSMo 441.234 at $300 or half of the periodic rent, whichever is greater, and never over one month's rent.

Which notice applies to your tenant?

It depends on why the landlord wants the tenant out. A landlord who is owed rent can skip the termination notice and go to court after demanding payment. A landlord ending a tenancy with no rent default must give a written notice that runs one month. Missouri sets these two tracks in RSMo 535.020 and RSMo 441.060.

For someone selling a rented house, the split decides the schedule. If the tenant is behind, the clock starts with a rent demand and a court filing. If the tenant is current and simply has to leave before closing, the clock starts with a written notice.

Rent demand before a nonpayment case

Under RSMo 535.020 the rent must have come due, the landlord or the landlord's agent must have demanded it from the tenant or whoever occupies the home, and it must remain unpaid. The landlord then signs an affidavit for an associate circuit judge listing the rental terms, the amount actually due, the demand, and a description of the property.

The same section says the landlord does not have to give the one-month notice from section 441.060 first. That is why a summons in a nonpayment case carries a court date no more than twenty-one business days out (RSMo 535.030), while a lease-ending notice alone takes a full month. RSMo 535.010 is the short rule behind it: when rent is not paid as agreed, the landlord may dispossess the tenant and any subtenants through the procedure in chapter 535.

A landlord may add other unpaid sums from the lease to the same case, but those sums are not rent, and a judgment for them alone does not entitle the landlord to possession.

Ending a month-to-month or at-will tenancy

One month, in writing. RSMo 441.060 lets the person entitled to possession end a tenancy at will, a tenancy by sufferance, or any tenancy for less than one year by giving one month's written notice telling the occupant to vacate.

An oral rental is treated as month to month under the same section, and either side may end it with one month's written notice. For month-to-month, the notice must say the tenancy ends on a rent-paying date at least one month after the other party receives it. A notice handed over on the 20th for a tenancy that renews on the 1st cannot end it on the very next 1st.

A tenant who owns the mobile home on a leased lot gets longer. The landlord must give written notice that the tenancy ends not sooner than sixty days from the date the next rent payment comes due, even if the lease says something shorter.

Other notices that start or end a tenancy

Three more notices come up often when a house is sold with someone living in it. Each has its own statute and its own count of days.

  • Foreclosure occupant notice. After a trustee's sale, the new owner must tell a former residential tenant that the sale happened and that the occupant has at least ten business days to leave. No possession action may start inside that window (RSMo 534.030).
  • Abandonment notice. If rent has gone unpaid for thirty days and the landlord reasonably believes the tenant left for good, the landlord may post a notice on the door and mail it by first class and certified mail. The tenant has ten days to answer in writing before the home can be treated as abandoned (RSMo 441.065).
  • Domestic violence protection. A tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking cannot be evicted for that reason. The statute also gives an affirmative defense to rent owed after the tenant moves out when the landlord was told and any requested documents were supplied (RSMo 441.920).

Notice periods at a glance

Missouri notice periods by situation
SituationNotice or waitStatute
Unpaid rentDemand for payment, then a verified statement filed with the court; no one-month notice needed535.020
Month-to-monthWritten notice ending on a rent-paying date at least one month after receipt441.060
Tenancy under one year, at willOne month's written notice441.060
Owner of a mobile home on a rented lotNot sooner than sixty days after the next rent date441.060
After a foreclosure saleAt least ten business days from the notice534.030
Suspected abandonmentThirty days unpaid, then ten days to respond to a posted and mailed notice441.065

Can a landlord skip court and remove a tenant?

No. RSMo 441.233 says a landlord or agent who removes or excludes a tenant or the tenant's belongings without judicial process and a court order, or who takes off doors or locks, is guilty of forcible entry and detainer under chapter 534. The same section covers willfully cutting electric, gas, water or sewer service, unless the landlord acts for health or safety reasons.

The one carve-out is the abandonment procedure in section 441.065. Outside that, a notice has to be followed by a judgment and an officer's writ before anyone is physically removed. An owner of a rented house should plan around that sequence and avoid promising a buyer an empty house on a fixed date.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Missouri houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling a rented Missouri house

A notice sets the earliest realistic date the house can be vacant, and a nonpayment filing sets a faster but less predictable one. A sale of an occupied house is allowed, so the choice is between waiting out the notice and selling with the tenant in place.

  • Read the lease first. A written lease for a year or more is not ended by the one-month notice that applies to shorter tenancies.
  • Ask the buyer in writing whether it will take the home with the tenant in it, and put the answer in the contract.
  • Keep copies of every notice, mailing receipt and posting, because the court will want proof of what was given and when.
  • Count business days and rent-paying dates, not calendar guesses, before setting a closing date.

Ask the circuit clerk in the county where the house sits which forms the local court expects for a rent and possession filing.

Timeline you can plan around

Working backward from a closing date helps. Decide first whether the tenant will stay or go. If the tenant is leaving and is current on rent, serve the written notice early enough that the end date falls on a rent-paying date well before closing. If the tenant is behind, make the demand, file, and allow for the court date, the days after judgment, and the officer's delivery of possession. A buyer who wants a clean, empty house should see this schedule in writing, and a cash buyer who accepts the house with the tenant still inside lets you skip most of it.

Frequently asked questions

How many days notice does a Missouri landlord have to give to evict for unpaid rent?

No set number of days applies to a rent case. After the landlord demands the rent and it stays unpaid, a verified statement can be filed with an associate circuit judge, and RSMo 535.020 says the one-month notice from section 441.060 is not required first.

Is one month's notice enough to end a month-to-month tenancy in Missouri?

Yes, if it is written and ends the tenancy on a rent-paying date at least one month after the other side receives it (RSMo 441.060). A notice that lands in the middle of a rental period usually pushes the end date to the next rent date.

What notice does a tenant get when the house is foreclosed on?

At least ten business days. The new owner must send the occupant a notice by certified or registered mail when the name is known, or regular mail addressed to Occupant when it is not, and post a copy on the door (RSMo 534.030). The notice does not create a tenancy.

Can a landlord throw a tenant's belongings out after a notice expires?

Not on a notice alone. Belongings left after a court-ordered execution fall under RSMo 535.040, and items clearly labeled as a third party's property must be offered back by certified mail with five business days to recover them. Belongings in a home that qualifies as abandoned follow RSMo 441.065.

Does a tenant who is a victim of domestic violence have special protection from eviction?

Yes. RSMo 441.920 bars eviction or a lease violation finding based on the tenant being, or being in imminent danger of becoming, a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, with exceptions when the tenant let the named person in or the landlord reasonably believes that person threatens other occupants or the property.

Who inherits a Missouri house when there is no will?

The answer turns on whether the owner left a spouse and whether any children came from outside that marriage. RSMo 474.010 sets the order of descent for property left without a will, and a house is divided under the same order as everything else in the estate.

A surviving spouse takes the whole intestate estate when the decedent had no surviving children or other issue. If there are children and every one of them is also the spouse's child, the spouse receives the first $20,000 plus half of what remains. If at least one child is not the spouse's, the spouse receives one half.

Whatever the spouse does not take, or the whole estate when there is no spouse, moves down a list:

  • the decedent's children, or their descendants, in equal parts;
  • if there are none, the parents, brothers and sisters or their descendants;
  • then grandparents, uncles and aunts or their descendants;
  • then great-grandparents and on to the nearest lineal ancestors and their descendants, with collateral relatives limited to the ninth degree of kinship.

If nobody qualifies, the property goes to the kindred of a predeceased spouse, and failing that it escheats. Co-heirs who inherit a house this way own it together, so a sale usually needs every one of them to sign.

Skipping full probate with a small estate affidavit

A small estate can pass by affidavit when everything left, after subtracting liens, debts and encumbrances, is $40,000 or less. RSMo 473.097 sets the conditions. Thirty days must have gone by since the death, with no application for letters pending or granted. A bond approved by the judge or clerk of the probate division must be filed, though the court may waive it. The filing fee, plus any newspaper publication cost, must be paid.

The person signing is the personal representative named in a probated will or, if there is none, a distributee. The affidavit describes and values the property, names who holds it and who will receive it, and states that debts and any estate tax will be paid. The clerk attaches a certificate naming the people entitled to each item. For a house, those people prove their right to the real estate by recording the affidavit and certificate with the recorder of deeds in each county where the land lies.

When the listed property is worth more than $15,000, the clerk publishes a notice to creditors once a week for two consecutive weeks. After the procedure is complete, the property cannot be taken in execution for the decedent's debts, although a secured creditor keeps its rights. Next to most house values, $40,000 is a low ceiling, so many estates that include a home will need letters from the court instead.

Deadlines for a will and for creditors

A will has no effect until it is presented to the probate division and admitted. Under RSMo 473.050, presenting means delivering the will, or a verified statement about a lost one, along with a petition or a small estate affidavit asking for admission. If no notice of the granting of letters has been given, the will must be presented within one year of the date of death. Once that notice has been published, the window is six months from first publication. A will that misses the time limit is barred from probate in Missouri.

Letters of administration run on a related clock. With limited exceptions, the court will not issue them unless the application comes within one year of death. Remember that number if an heir ends up with a house years after a parent died and nothing was ever filed.

Creditors have their own limit. RSMo 473.444 makes most claims against a decedent unenforceable one year after death, whether or not an estate was opened and whether or not the creditor knew. Costs of administration, exempt property, family and homestead allowances, claims of the United States and claims of any taxing authority are carved out. A mortgage or other lien on the property can still be enforced, so a lienholder on the house is a separate matter from an unsecured creditor.

Who can sign a deed to sell an inherited house?

Who may sign depends on how the estate is being handled. When the court has issued letters, the personal representative acts for the estate. When a small estate affidavit is used, the distributees named in the clerk's certificate record that paperwork and then hold title for the sale. A buyer or title company will want to see whichever document applies before it insures the sale.

One workaround is worth knowing. RSMo 461.025 allows a beneficiary deed, a deed that states it does not take effect until the owner dies. It transfers the interest to the named grantee at death if it was signed and filed with the recorder of deeds before the owner died. It needs no consideration, it does not have to be delivered to the grantee, and it can name a trust as the grantee. A deed that is valid on other grounds is not defeated just because it was recorded after the owner's death.

The county circuit court's probate division handles letters, small estate affidavits and creditor notices. Ask that court's clerk for the local filing steps and fee schedule, since procedures are applied county by county.

Steps before selling an inherited house

Begin by finding out whether a will exists and whether it was presented to the probate division in time. Then work out the value of the whole estate after liens, because that figure decides whether the small estate route is open. The mortgage balance and any other lien on the home reduce the number for that test. Ownership held jointly with right of survivorship sits outside the decedent's property for the affidavit.

  • Order certified death certificates and gather the deed, the mortgage statement and the latest tax bill.
  • Ask the probate clerk whether letters have been requested and whether the one-year application window is still open.
  • List every heir in line under RSMo 474.010 if no will exists, since each one may need to sign.
  • Record the affidavit and clerk's certificate with the county recorder of deeds before listing or closing, if the small estate route applies.
  • Check for open claims against the estate while the one-year creditor limit is running.

Paperwork differs by county, so call the probate division clerk and the recorder of deeds before you list. It saves weeks later. A cash sale of an inherited house still needs clean authority to sign, but it skips repairs, showings and the wait for a buyer's financing, which can matter when several heirs live in different places.

Frequently asked questions

What is the largest estate that can use the Missouri small estate affidavit?

The ceiling is $40,000 after subtracting liens, debts and encumbrances. RSMo 473.097 also requires a thirty-day wait after the death, with no application for letters pending or granted, a bond unless the court waives it, and payment of the fee.

Does a surviving spouse inherit everything in Missouri?

Only when the decedent left no surviving children or other issue. If all the children are also the spouse's, the spouse takes the first $20,000 plus half of the rest, and if any child is from another relationship the spouse takes half.

How long do I have to present a will to the court?

Within one year of death when no notice of letters has been given, or six months after first publication of notice of letters. A will that misses its window is barred, and letters of administration generally require an application within one year of death.

Do I have to record anything with the county to sell inherited land?

If the small estate affidavit is used, yes. The distributees record a copy of the affidavit and the clerk's certificate with the recorder of deeds in each county where the property sits.

Can an owner avoid probate for a house before dying?

A beneficiary deed under RSMo 461.025 can. It must say it is not to take effect until the owner's death and be filed with the recorder of deeds in the county where the property sits before the owner dies.
